title: Random numbers and their tests
subtitle: Computers cannot be random, so we build generators whose output passes every test for randomness we can think of.

sections.title: What we need from a generator
sections.body:
Here is a secret that surprises most people: your computer cannot truly roll a die. It follows instructions, and instructions are never random. So what do we mean by a random number generator? We want numbers that look uniformly distributed on [0, 1) and independent.

There are practical needs, too: fast, reproducible (same seed, same stream, which is essential for debugging), a long period before repeating, and the ability to produce several independent streams. Since an algorithm produces them they are pseudo-random. Why is reproducibility desirable in simulation? So that you can rerun a strange result exactly and find the bug.

questions.prompt: Why is reproducibility (a seed) desirable in simulation?

choices.text: You can rerun exactly the same experiment to debug or compare designs fairly.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Common random numbers reduce variance between compared systems.

keynotes: We want numbers that look uniformly distributed on [0, 1) and independent.
Practical needs: fast, reproducible (same seed, same stream), a long period before repeating, and several independent streams.
Since an algorithm produces them they are pseudo-random.

sections.title: The linear congruential method
sections.body:
The classic recipe is a one-line wonder: Xn+1 = (a·Xn + c) mod m, with Un = Xn/m. Try it. With a = 5, c = 3, m = 16, X₀ = 7: X₁ = (5·7 + 3) mod 16 = 38 mod 16 = 6; X₂ = (5·6 + 3) mod 16 = 33 mod 16 = 1. The whole sequence is 7 6 1 8 11 10 5 12 15 14 9 0 3 2 13 4 7, which visits all 16 values before repeating (full period yes).

But choose the constants badly and it cycles early. The Hull–Dobell theorem tells you when you get a full period m: c and m are coprime, a−1 is divisible by every prime factor of m, and by 4 if m is divisible by 4. A poor choice (a = 4, c = 0, m = 16, X₀ = 1) has a period of 1... it repeats almost immediately, as the second figure shows. A multiplicative (c = 0) generator can reach at most m−1. The maximum possible period of an LCG with modulus m is m.

questions.prompt: The maximum possible period of an LCG with modulus m is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: There are only m distinct states.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The state is one number below m.

problems.prompt: Generate the first 6 numbers for X₀ = 7, a = 5, c = 3, m = 16 and find the period.

keynotes: The linear congruential method is X(n+1) = (a·X(n) + c) mod m with U(n) = X(n)/m.
With a = 5, c = 3, m = 16, X₀ = 7 the sequence 7 6 1 8 11 10 5 12 15 14 9 0 3 2 13 4 7 has full period.
Hull–Dobell: full period m iff c and m are coprime, a−1 is divisible by every prime factor of m, and by 4 if m is divisible by 4.

sections.title: Testing uniformity: χ² and Kolmogorov–Smirnov
sections.body:
You have built a generator; how do you check that its numbers look uniform? Two standard tests. The chi-square test splits [0,1) into k classes and compares observed counts Oᵢ with the expected n/k: χ² = Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ. Reject uniformity if it exceeds the critical value for k−1 degrees of freedom (14.07 for 8 classes at 5%).

The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test compares the empirical CDF with the ideal diagonal: D = max gap, with critical value ≈ 1.36/√n. For the full-period generator here, χ² = 0 and D = 0.0625. A significance level of 5% means you accept a 5% chance of wrongly rejecting a good generator.

questions.prompt: A significance level of 5% in a randomness test means…

choices.text: A good generator is wrongly rejected about 5% of the time.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The level is the false-rejection rate.

keynotes: The chi-square test compares observed counts with the expected n/k: χ² = Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ, with critical value 14.07 for 8 classes at 5%.

sections.title: Other tests: gap, poker, autocorrelation
sections.body:
Uniform is not the same as random. The sequence 0.1, 0.2, 0.3… is perfectly uniform and perfectly predictable. So you also need tests of independence. The gap test: gaps between occurrences of a digit should be geometric. The poker test: frequencies of patterns such as all different, one pair, three of a kind. Runs tests: lengths of ascending or descending runs. And autocorrelation: the correlation between Ui and Ui+k should be near 0.

Do the poker test on 3-digit groups. The probability all three digits differ = 10·9·8/10³ = 0.72. Exactly one pair: 3·10·9/10³ = 0.27; all same 10/10³ = 0.01. Total 0.72 + 0.27 + 0.01 = 1. The sequence 0.1, 0.2, … 0.9 fails the tests of independence, such as the runs test.

worked.why: Poker test on 3-digit groups: probability all three digits differ = 10·9·8/10³.
Exactly one pair: 3·10·9/10³ = 0.27; all same 10/10³ = 0.01. Total 1.00.

questions.prompt: The sequence 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, …, 0.9 fails which kind of test?

choices.text: Independence — consecutive values are perfectly correlated.

keynotes: Uniformity is not enough: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3… is uniform but not random.
Independence tests are the gap test, poker test, runs tests and autocorrelation (U_i against U_(i+k) near 0).
In the poker test on 3-digit groups, all different is 0.72, exactly one pair 0.27 and all same 0.01.

sections.title: Generating other distributions
sections.body:
From one flat stream of uniform numbers, how do you get an exponential, or any other shape? Given U ~ Uniform(0,1), the inverse transform method sets X = F⁻¹(U). For the exponential with rate λ, F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx), so X = −ln(1−U)/λ.

Try it for λ = 2 and U = 0.6: X = −ln(1−0.6)/2, and ln 0.4 = −0.916, so X = 0.916/2 = 0.458. Other methods: rejection sampling, composition (mix distributions) and convolution (sum of variables: Erlang = sum of exponentials). For discrete values, divide [0,1) into intervals of the given probabilities. Inverse transform produces X from U by applying the inverse of the CDF.

worked.why: Generate an exponential(λ = 2) variate from U = 0.6.

questions.prompt: The inverse-transform method produces X from U by…

choices.text: Applying the inverse CDF, X = F⁻¹(U).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The CDF maps X to uniform, so its inverse maps uniform to X.

keynotes: The inverse transform method sets X = F⁻¹(U); for the exponential with rate λ, X = −ln(1−U)/λ.
Other methods are rejection sampling, composition (mix distributions) and convolution (Erlang = sum of exponentials).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Three lines, and then on to the last stretch.

  • LCG: X ← (aX + c) mod m; full period needs Hull–Dobell.
  • Test uniformity (χ², KS) and independence (runs, gaps, autocorrelation).
  • Inverse transform: X = F⁻¹(U).
keynotes: An LCG is X ← (aX + c) mod m, and full period needs the Hull–Dobell conditions.
Test uniformity with χ² and KS, and independence with runs, gaps and autocorrelation.
The inverse transform is X = F⁻¹(U).
